name: Standard Scramble

pitch_detail.notes: Initial alpine terrain above the high camp; mostly straightforward scrambling on solid granite. Good rock quality, solid.
Transitional section with some slab scrambling. Rock is clean granite slabs interspersed with blocky sections. Route-finding begins.
Steeper section with krummholz and bluffs. Requires careful foot placement on loose, vegetation-covered rock. Crux of standard route.
Southwest ridge section with moderate slopes. Rock quality remains good. Teetering blocks near summit require caution.
Final push to summit across moderate slopes. Exposed windy section with excellent views of Pasayten peaks and Canadian ranges.

descent_text: There is no rappelling on this route — it is a walk-off/downclimb descent that simply reverses the ascent line. From the summit, downclimb the class 2-3 ground back to the notch on the southwest ridge at ~7,600 ft, then descend the same steep heather/talus/scree slope back into the Freezeout Creek drainage. This is the point where parties get into trouble: the upper basin has several gullies and chutes that look similar from above, and dropping into the wrong one risks cliffing out on bluffs well above the creek — stick to the exact ascent gully rather than improvising a shortcut. Cross back to the west side of Freezeout Creek at about 5,000 ft, follow the creek down through the old burn, rejoin the Freezeout Creek Trail tread around 4,200 ft, pass back through the cabin at 3,600 ft, and continue down to the abandoned lower Freezeout Creek Trail / Lightning Creek Trail junction, watching again for the flagged diagonal line through the steep rock-and-alder section. Finish on the Lightning Creek Trail back to the Ross Lake shoreline for the return boat/water-taxi pickup. Because of the length of the day, parties commonly finish this descent in the dark (one party that brought its own boat reached the lakeshore around 11:30pm after a roughly 4am start; the water taxi runs only from 8am to 5pm), so carry headlamps and treat the unmaintained trail sections and creek crossings with extra caution when tired and in low light. Other hazards on the way down include loose, ball-bearing-like scree on the upper slopes (slip/fall risk), the creek crossings themselves if water is high, and afternoon thunderstorm/lightning exposure on the open summit ridge and upper basin — get off the ridge before storms build.
approach: This route starts with a boat crossing of Ross Lake (Ross Lake Resort water taxi, or a private/inflatable boat carried in via the 0.6-mile portage trail from the SR-20 pullout), landing at the Lightning Creek Trailhead near the head of the lake at roughly 1,500 ft. From the shoreline, follow the Lightning Creek Trail north; parties with their own boat commonly start pre-dawn (around 4am) to leave enough daylight for the long day above, while the water taxi runs only from 8am to 5pm. After about 2 hours of hiking, watch for the junction with the old, no-longer-maintained Freezeout Creek Trail. The first stretch above the junction is the trickiest routefinding on the whole approach: steep rock-and-alder slopes that require a rising, diagonal ascent line before you regain proper forest and trail tread — recent parties note intermittent orange flagging tape marking this stretch, which is worth watching for. Once back in the trees, tread on the Freezeout Creek Trail improves to 'decent shape' as you climb to the Freezeout Cabin at about 3,600 ft, sited immediately after a creek crossing; the cabin (maintained bunks, wood stove, logbook) is a good psychological waypoint and emergency shelter. About a quarter mile past the cabin, cross Freezeout Creek again and pass through an old burn. Trail tread mostly disappears around 4,200 ft, but the bushwhacking through here is described as minimal. From there, stay on the west side of Freezeout Creek, hiking roughly 50-100 ft above the waterline, which gives the most open going through 5,000 ft. At 5,000 ft, cross to the south/east side of the drainage, where the terrain opens into meadow and talus. Above this, climb steep red heather, talus, and scree to a notch on the peak's southwest ridge at about 7,600 ft. From the notch, the final roughly 700-750 vertical feet to the 8,300+ ft summit is class 2 with short class 3 sections. Total one-way distance from the lakeshore to the summit is on the order of 16-17 miles with close to 7,000 ft of gain from the boat landing alone (the 8,500 ft gain figure reflects the day's cumulative up-and-down, not just net elevation). Freezeout Creek is the reliable water source for essentially the entire approach up to about 5,000-5,500 ft; carry water above that, since there is no dependable source on the upper heather/talus/scree slopes or the summit ridge. Because of the remoteness and boat-access logistics, this is realistically a long single push (18+ hours car-to-car including the taxi) or a one-night backpack, not a casual day hike.
overview: Castle Peak (8,343 ft; a 2020s survey pegged it at 8343.4 ft +/- 0.2 ft) is the second-highest summit in the Hozameen Range after Jack Mountain and the 6th-highest peak in the Pasayten Wilderness, about 1 mile south of the Canada-US border on the Cascade crest (Okanogan/Whatcom county line). With roughly 3,263 ft of prominence it ranks 42nd in Washington and is one of the state's most remote high-prominence summits (distinct from the Tatoosh Range's Castle Peak). It is granite; the peak's steep north face holds several technical routes up to IV 5.10+ A1 (e.g. 'The Drawbridge'; the north face proper was first climbed by Beckey-Nolting-Tindall in 1979), while the standard route is an unroped class 2-3 scramble up the southwest side, reached by long, remote approaches.
beta: Castle Peak's standard ascent is a granite scramble featuring mostly Class 2 terrain with sections of easy Class 3. Rock quality is excellent and reminiscent of the Stuart Range. Route-finding is required in micro-terrain and sections are steep with krummholz. The peak can be approached from three main directions, all requiring significant approach commitment.
fa: 1904 USGS Survey party (first ascent of peak)
face: Southwest Ridge via a notch at ~7,600 ft above the Freezeout Creek basin
